headline: Instinct AI holds its own against OpenAI, Meta agents
summary: Despite competition from tech giants, the buzzy AI startup's focus on personal assistance and a text-based interface is helping it stand out.
details: Instinct AI, a startup that gained significant buzz through an invite-only approach and minimal marketing, is proving its mettle against AI heavyweights like OpenAI and Meta. Praised for its straightforward, text message-based interface, Instinct can handle everyday tasks such as booking appointments and sending follow-up emails.

The company, valued at $10 billion in September, differentiates itself by focusing solely on building a personal assistant for everyday life. Founder Noah Shinn believes this singular focus sets Instinct apart from larger companies developing AI products for a broader range of customers.

Unlike competitors with mascots or anthropomorphized interfaces, Instinct communicates through text messages via iMessage, WhatsApp, or email. This minimalist approach, devoid of a traditional app, allows the AI to be accessible anywhere text messages can be sent, including on car systems and smartwatches.

Instinct's AI agent can perform life admin tasks, similar to agents like Muse and Dots, by accessing a virtual machine and integrating with personal email and calendars. Users can connect it to services like Google Workspace, Slack, and Notion, and provide website login details through a secure vault.

While the AI's ability to perform tasks in the real world has limitations, its seamless integration into daily communication channels is seen as a key advantage. The startup aims to turn conversation into action, making the AI a quiet, ever-present helper rather than a distinct application.

headline: Meta bans TikTok ads across its platforms amid escalating rivalry
summary: The social media giant has restricted ads from ByteDance and third-party ads linking to TikTok in the US and several other countries.
details: Meta has officially banned ads from TikTok's parent company, ByteDance, across the US and multiple other countries. This move signifies a significant escalation in the ongoing rivalry between the two major social media operators.

The restriction, which went into effect on Thursday, prohibits all ads and paid marketing messages originating from ByteDance. It also extends to third-party advertisements that direct users to TikTok.

A Meta spokesperson stated, "We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps. Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries."

This decision follows Meta's recent $17 billion child safety settlement and its calls for TikTok and YouTube to implement similar safeguards. TikTok reportedly declined to run Meta's ad campaign on its platform.

The ban impacts ad placements in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand, and Vietnam. While TikTok in the US is now majority-owned by US-based companies, ByteDance remains a significant shareholder.
